title: Capacity, Queues, and Tail Latency
readiness_note: Ready on 2026-07-31 after course validation, 22 lab tests, resource verification, two independent evaluator runs per fixture, and deterministic calibration checking passed.

outcomes.statement: Model logical work, attempts, operation mix, normal, peak, burst, projected, skewed, and recovery demand with visible uncertainty.
Calculate concurrency, per-resource service demand, nominal capacity, and failover exposure using consistent boundaries.
Implement and test fixed workers, explicit bounded waiting, fan-out, downstream admission, logical identities, and timing instrumentation.
Design an open-loop latency experiment that exposes coordinated omission, generator limits, rejection, and uncertainty.
Predict and measure fan-out tail amplification, downstream branch demand, and correlation limits.
Locate saturation from useful throughput, latency, queue, rejection, concurrency, and generator evidence across the required load sweep.
Keep overload, priority, retries, downstream work, and recovery bounded under burst and dependency failure.
Defend a workload-scoped safe operating region, actionable scaling signal, overload policy, failover reserve, ownership model, and cost per useful request.

resources.title: Queueing Systems lecture notes
resources.author_or_publisher: Richard C. Larson, Amedeo R. Odoni, Arnold Barnett; MIT OpenCourseWare
resources.purpose: Distinguish Little's Law from a full queueing prediction.
resources.assignment: Study queue terminology, Little's Law, dynamic behavior, and strengths/weaknesses; skip Markov derivations. Explain one invalid use and calculate one boundary two ways.

resources.title: The Tail at Scale
resources.author_or_publisher: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso; Google Research
resources.purpose: Connect branch variance and fan-out to user-journey latency.
resources.assignment: Read the complete article. Choose one tail technique and state its extra work, correctness assumption, and rejection condition.

resources.title: Addressing Cascading Failures
resources.author_or_publisher: Mike Ulrich and Google SRE contributors; Google
resources.purpose: Relate finite resources and retry feedback to overload controls.
resources.assignment: Read Resource Exhaustion, Queue Management, Load Shedding and Graceful Degradation, and Retries. Draw one retry feedback loop and its earliest control.

resources.title: Avoiding Insurmountable Queue Backlogs
resources.purpose: Treat backlog recovery as capacity work with a clearance objective.
resources.assignment: Read the complete article. Calculate net drain and clearance for one backlog and identify the fragile assumption.

resources.title: HdrHistogram README
resources.author_or_publisher: Gil Tene, Michael Barker, and HdrHistogram maintainers
resources.purpose: Understand coordinated omission and corrected recording.
resources.assignment: Read the overview and Corrected vs. Raw value recording calls. Describe missing arrivals under a ten-second closed-loop stall.

resources.title: How to Trade off Server Utilization and Tail Latency
resources.purpose: Build intuition for utilization and waiting-time distributions.
resources.assignment: Watch the complete presentation or read all slides with speaker notes. Explain why run at 80% is not a general policy.

resources.title: Timeouts, Retries, and Backoff with Jitter
resources.purpose: Extend the bounded retry model toward Module 6.
resources.assignment: Optional: read the complete article and record one timeout failure and one question for Module 6.

failure_experiments.evidence: Branch and journey distributions, useful throughput, correlation limits, and prediction comparison
Intended/actual arrivals, queue age/depth, rejection, user latency, and recovery
Queue wait, deadline exposure, rejection trade-off, memory bound, and recovery debt
Originals, attempts, recovered unique work, budget use/denial, and downstream effect
Atomic reservation, cheap denial, downstream peak, hidden-wait audit, and protected work
Retained capacity, safe range, shedding, backlog clearance, cost, and recovery owner

challenge_questions.prompt: Which claim in your artifact most directly supports this outcome, and what evidence could falsify it: Model logical work, attempts, operation mix, normal, peak, burst, projected, skewed, and recovery demand with visible uncertainty.

What unstated assumption could invalidate your treatment of this outcome, and how would you test it: Calculate concurrency, per-resource service demand, nominal capacity, and failover exposure using consistent boundaries.

Defend the causal chain behind your evidence for this outcome, including the first likely failure: Implement and test fixed workers, explicit bounded waiting, fan-out, downstream admission, logical identities, and timing instrumentation.

Which reasonable alternative would challenge your treatment of this outcome, and under what evidence would it win: Design an open-loop latency experiment that exposes coordinated omission, generator limits, rejection, and uncertainty.

What operational, security, cost, or ownership consequence is least supported in your treatment of this outcome: Predict and measure fan-out tail amplification, downstream branch demand, and correlation limits.

Where does your evidence stop transferring to production for this outcome, and how is that boundary disclosed: Locate saturation from useful throughput, latency, queue, rejection, concurrency, and generator evidence across the required load sweep.

What dissent should a skeptical reviewer raise about your treatment of this outcome, and what follow-up evidence would resolve it: Keep overload, priority, retries, downstream work, and recovery bounded under burst and dependency failure.

What changed belief or reversal condition follows from your work on this outcome, and where is it recorded: Defend a workload-scoped safe operating region, actionable scaling signal, overload policy, failover reserve, ownership model, and cost per useful request.
